state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think about what the range represents in this context. The range is the difference between the tallest and shortest plant heights. If all the plants were cut in half or grew by the same amount, how would that affect the difference between the tallest and shortest plant heights? Let's explore this idea further together.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh right, so if they all grew by 3 cm, the tallest would still be 3 cm taller than the shortest, so the range would stay the same... but wait, if we cut them all in half, wouldn't that make the difference smaller? I'm confused now because I thought Tom was right, but maybe Katie is actually right instead?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: You're on the right track with thinking about how cutting the plants in half would affect the range. Think about how each plant's new height would compare to the others if they were all cut in half. This might help you see whether the range would change or stay the same.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher maintains cognitive demand by asking the student to reason about range, but fails to address the specific misconception about proportional changes, and the student ends up more confused, moving from the correct answer (Katie) toward the incorrect one (Tom) by Turn 2, with no clear resolution by the end.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher effectively scaffolds by breaking down the concept of range, prompts the student to explore both scenarios systematically, and adjusts support in Turn 3 by directing attention to the cutting-in-half case when the student shows confusion, though could have been slightly more explicit in guiding the mathematical comparison.
